proof:
# Exact trimmed target family and endpoint-selection optimality

This is an n=1 transport reduction. It allows nonuniform endpoint
submeasures and distributed residual targets. It neither prescribes a
log-concave target nor tries to collapse all residual mass to an atom.

## 1. Eliminate central-central pairs exactly

Normalize the mixed measure mu to mass one, and write L,R,w for its strict
left, strict right, and median-fiber masses. Thus L,R<=1/2 and
L+R+w=1. Assume w<1/2. For the probability half-marginals alpha,beta,

    alpha_L=2 mu_L,       mass(alpha_0)=1-2L,
    beta_R=2 mu_R,        mass(beta_0)=1-2R.

Their central measures are proportional to mu_0 and sum to 2mu_0. Define
r=1-2w>0. Choose ANY finite measure rho on strict-left times strict-right
with mass r and marginals dominated by alpha_L,beta_R. Such measures exist,
since r<=2L,2R; proportional submarginals followed by product coupling give
one example.

The unused strict-left marginal has mass

    2L-r=1-2R=mass(beta_0),

and the unused strict-right marginal has mass 1-2L=mass(alpha_0).
Couple these remainders to the opposite central measures arbitrarily.
Together with rho this is a complete coupling with no central-central
pairs. Every central/noncentral pair maps to its central endpoint, so
its target probability is exactly

    nu=2mu_0+T#rho.                                      (1)

Conversely every coupling having no central-central pairs has this form:
its strict-cross block has mass r by the marginal identities, and the
other blocks contribute precisely 2mu_0. Thus (1) characterizes the entire
trimmed target family, not merely one construction.

## 2. The three-fiber form

For three consecutive fibers A,B,C at -1,0,1, use unnormalized volumes
a,b,c and M=a+b+c. The median and nonheavy conditions say

    a,c<=M/2,       b<M/2.

Put m=(a+c-b)/2, so 0<m<=min(a,c). Multiplying (1) by M/2 shows that the
unnormalized target measures are exactly

    lambda=1_B dx+T#pi,       T(x,x')=(x+x')/2,          (2)

where pi has mass m and marginals dominated by 1_A dx and 1_C dx. Every
such pi is permitted. Minkowski compatibility ensures T(A,C) is contained
in B, so lambda is supported in B and has mass b+m=M/2. The normalized
probability is nu=lambda/(b+m).

The endpoint submarginals may be selected freely and need not be uniform
on convex subsets. Their unused parts are absorbed by central-endpoint
pairings, whose target contribution has already been fixed to uniform B.

## 3. Compactness and finite cap duals

The partial coupling set

    P_m={pi>=0: mass(pi)=m, pi_X<=1_A dx, pi_Y<=1_C dx}

is weakly compact. Domination is closed when tested against nonnegative
continuous functions, and A times C is compact. Closed-halfspace target
masses are upper semicontinuous, including their moving-center versions.
Consequently the maximum target depth over pi and center y in B is
attained, as in the full-coupling argument.

For a fixed y, put b_H=|B intersect H| and
c_H(x,x')=1_H((x+x')/2), for closed halfspaces H through y. The unnormalized
fixed-center depth optimum is

    W(y)=max_(pi in P_m) inf_H [b_H+integral c_H d pi].

For every epsilon>0 a finite list H_i gives an upper approximation within
epsilon, and its exact dual is

    min_(theta_i>=0, sum theta_i=1)
       [sum_i theta_i b_(H_i)
           +max_(pi in P_m) integral c_theta d pi],
    c_theta=sum_i theta_i c_(H_i).                      (3)

Both finite extrema are attained. The compact finite-intersection and
downward-payoff separation proofs from
`candidate 641c5559a440bf48` apply without change, including
the constants b_H. A globally optimal pi at its chosen center is therefore
epsilon-optimal for a finite step-cost PARTIAL transport problem (3).

## 4. Free endpoint selection gives additional exact inequalities

Let pi in P_m be epsilon-optimal for maximizing a bounded Borel cost c.
Write

    ell=1_A dx-pi_X,        r=1_C dx-pi_Y,
    l=mass(ell)=a-m,        s=mass(r)=c-m.

Then the following quantitative inequalities hold:

 integral [c(p',q)-c(p,q)]_+ d pi(p,q)d ell(p')
       <=max(m,l) epsilon,                              (4)

 integral [c(p,q')-c(p,q)]_+ d pi(p,q)d r(q')
       <=max(m,s) epsilon,                              (5)

 integral [c(p',q')-c(p,q)]_+
                      d pi(p,q)d ell(p')d r(q')
       <=max(ls,ms,ml) epsilon.                         (6)

If an unused mass is zero, the corresponding integrals vanish. For exact
optimality these imply the pointwise nonpositivity of each gain almost
everywhere for its displayed product measure. They are selection conditions,
not merely cyclic swaps among already selected endpoints.

To prove (4), restrict pi times ell to any measurable set E of triples.
Project it onto the old pair (p,q) and onto the new pair (p',q), obtaining
eta_old and eta_new. The old pair measure is bounded by l pi. The new
first marginal is bounded by m ell, and the second marginal is unchanged.
Hence replacing t eta_old by t eta_new is feasible for
t=1/max(m,l) when max(m,l)>0: old removal is dominated by pi, new left
mass is dominated by the available ell, and the right constraint is
unchanged. The selected total mass remains m. Take E where the gain is
positive and use epsilon-optimality. This proves (4), and (5) is symmetric.

For (6), restrict pi times ell times r to a set of quadruples. The old
pair projection is bounded by ls pi; the new left marginal is bounded by
ms ell and its new right marginal by ml r. Scaling by
1/max(ls,ms,ml), when nonzero, makes the replacement feasible. Choose the
positive-gain set as before. No support regularity or continuity of c is
used.

The ordinary cyclic-swap inequalities also remain available. With k pairs
sampled from the mass-m measure pi, their quantitative right side is
k m^(k-1) epsilon, using the same restricted-product replacement proof.

## 5. The atom-preserving center repair respects the trim constraint

The full target construction can also be viewed as a coupling with the
closed forbidden block central times central removed. Under a common
continuous translation, retain the valid pairs exactly as in
`candidate e2ef40d391cd1f07`. If e is the discarded pair
mass, the sum of the two residual central marginal masses is at most e:
every removed pair had at most one central endpoint.

Two residual probability-side marginals of common mass e admit a coupling
avoiding the central-central block whenever the sum of their central
masses is at most e. Explicitly pair each central part with a sufficiently
large opposite strict part, and pair the remaining strict parts together.
Thus the marginal deficits can be repaired without leaving the trim family.

The optimized trimmed fixed-center depth, and its finite transport
capacities, inherit the same atom-preserving center-translation Lipschitz
bound as the full family. This controls continuity but does not assert
concavity, log-concavity, or the required gamma_d lower bound.

## 6. Unused endpoint supports force a large low-cost region

Let pi be an EXACT maximizer for a finite cap mixture

    c(x)=sum_i theta_i 1_(H_i)(x),

evaluated at the midpoint T. Let r0 be the essential infimum of c(T)
under pi. Because the cost has only finitely many values, the selected
set where c(T)=r0 has positive pi mass. Suppose both unused masses l,s
from Section 4 are positive, and write U=supp(ell), V=supp(r). Then

    c_open((u+v)/2)<=r0      for every u in U, v in V,    (7)

where c_open uses the interiors of the same cap halfspaces.

Indeed the exact version of (6), restricted to the positive selected set
where c(T)=r0, gives c((u+v)/2)<=r0 for ell times r almost every pair.
The open-cap cost is lower semicontinuous and no greater than c. If it
exceeded r0 at a pair in U times V, it would do so on a product
neighborhood of positive ell times r measure, a contradiction. This proves
(7), including the support-boundary points.

The two unused measures have densities at most one, so |U|>=l and
|V|>=s. Their Minkowski average lies in B by compatibility. Brunn-Minkowski
and (7) therefore give the exact geometric bound

    |B intersect {c<=r0}|
       >=[(l^(1/d)+s^(1/d))/2]^d.                       (8)

To pass from c_open to c, discard the finitely many cap boundary
hyperplanes, which have d-dimensional volume zero. The supports U,V are
compact measurable sets; no assertion that they are convex is needed for
the ordinary Brunn-Minkowski inequality. This supplies a geometric
consequence of free endpoint selection, but (8) alone is not the desired
gamma_d estimate.
